Posted March 26, 2003
Analysis by Richard Cowan

Almost two years ago I wrote about how actions by the Bush administration had changed the global climate for prohibition.
See
 Bush Changes the Global Climate for Marijuana Prohibition. Analysis by Richard Cowan

That was all very minor in comparison with what is happening now.

All wars have unintended consequences. Indeed, the Iraq war is an unintended consequence of the First World War, and of the 1991 Gulf War.

The interesting thing about the Iraq war is just how many unintended consequences hit even before the shooting started. It will be years after the shooting stops before we know all of the consequences of the war, good, bad, or both.

(Please note that this has nothing to do with whether one thinks that the Iraq war is a good or bad idea, or both. All that is important in this context is what other countries think about it, and how the Bush administration reacts to these countries.)

Starting closest to home, both Mexico and Canada have opposed Bush on the war. In Mexico's case this is just a return to the historic mild anti-gringoism that has been a political staple since The Revolution. It is notable only because Vincente Fox was supposed to be Bush's new best friend, until Bush couldn't deliver immigration reform from the post-9/11 Congress.

However, in Canada's case it is rather more serious. Although Canada has taken independent foreign policy positions in the past, notably on Cuba, the real problem is that the Chretien government has handled the matter very badly.
See
 Canadian Prime Minister Says He Has Been In Favor Of Decrim Since 1980. How Time Flies When You Are In Power. Possession Law Hostage to Medical Cannabis. Another Deadline On Taking Care of Patients.

Ironically, even as the DEAland ambassador, former Massachusetts governor Paul Celucci, is complaining about the degree of anti-Americanism in the Canadian opposition to the war, Canada has about as many assets in the area as it would if it were a belligerent. It actually has people on the staff at Doha and a few special forces that may even be in Iraq. It also has ships in the area to fight terrorism, just in case Osama has a navy that we have overlooked.

The Canadian conservatives and the business community are worried about how this is going to affect trade. This, of course, echoes the concerns raised about how DEAland would react to Canada changing its cannabis policies.
See
 Walters Concedes That Canada Can Legalize Cannabis If It Wants To, Which Was The Only True Thing He Said While In Montreal.

Cannabis is no longer the biggest concern by any means. Frankly, I have always thought that this was a bit of a red herring, inasmuch as trade is a two way street, literally. The fact is that American multinationals are integrated across the border and would be badly hurt by any interference in trade, and Canada is a major supplier of oil and an important source of electricity.

In any case, it is hard to see how the Canadian government could say that they cannot change their cannabis policies for fear of offending the Bush administration, after they have so rudely opposed them on the supposedly much more important Iraqi war.

However, they might think that the Bush administration places more importance on suppressing cannabis than anything else, so Canada has to keep arresting its own citizens to appease the crazy neighbors. And they might be right.
See
 The Ultimate Betrayal: Depriving Our Troops of Medical Cannabis. But It Is Okay to Give Combat Pilots Speed. US Army Tests Proved Cannabis Works Four Years Ago!
and
 The Endless Cynicism of the Drug Warriors. The Drug War and Terrorism. MarijuanaNews Analysis by Richard Cowan

And that is where Mexico comes in with a few embarrassing facts for the prohibitionists. As noted, Mexico is also opposing the war, but it is also a very important trading partner, and a major oil supplier. It also happens to be the real source of almost all of the imported cannabis in DEAland.
See
 How Marijuana Prohibition Really Works on the Texas/Mexico Border. Contrast with the Situation at the Canadian Border. Great Journalism.

Moreover, Mexico is even more sensitive to any perceived threat to its sovereignty than is Canada. So now our two neighbors are in this together, and that is really something new.

Canadian prohibitionists like to complain that they have to suppress cannabis cultivation because it is run by organized crime and it is all smuggled into DEAland. That is mostly untrue for Canada, but it is mostly true for Mexico. The fact is that both countries, but especially Mexico, are victims of the DEAland drug war, and the game of blaming the victims is breeding resentment in the rest of the world.

Which takes us even further south

DEAland involvement in Colombia is finally generating opposition in Congress. It is the third largest recipient of DEAland foreign aid but it's long running civil war is fed mostly by the profits from cocaine. Of course, it is not alone in having this problem. In the Andes, the Drug War is a war in the most literal sense.
See
 Is the War On Drugs A Just War. "? Should It Be Easier To Justify Violence Against A Foreign Dictatorship Than Against Peaceful Citizens Of One's Own Country?

A leftist party supported by peasants who want to grow coca nearly overthrew the Bolivian government recently. (The current president got just 22% of the vote, which makes Bush's victory look like a landslide!)

It would be nice if the peace movement would notice what DEAland is doing to some of the poorest people in the world, including what amounts to chemical warfare against the cannabis growers in Mexico and coca growers in the Andes.

And perhaps after the shooting stops in Iraq they will finally notice. Although DEAland is the major supporter of the drug war, it is hardly alone. France is very prohibitionist, as are most of the Third World dictatorships in the UN.
See
 UN Nark's Speech To Swedish Prohibitionists May Cause Permanent Brain Damage. Illogic, Ignorance and Lying, Especially About the Dutch, Of Course.

However, inasmuch as cannabis suppression in particular is identified with DEAland it is going to be increasingly difficult to sell a US-style Drug War to centrist governments in Europe.

Ideologues like John Walters will be recognized as precisely the sort of absurd ideologue that opponents of the Iraq war identify with the heavy-handedness of the Bush policies.

Early in April there is a meeting in Vienna about the future of the various anti-drug treaties. There will be no changes at this time, but the prohibitionists are in a major panic over the idea that anyone is even thinking about it. They are no longer sacred.
See
 Swiss Government Says Going Dutch Does NOT Violate Treaties. Implications for Other Countries, Especially Canada and UK. Plus Full Text of UN Nark Press Release.

When the dust settles in Baghdad, we can take another look at the rest of the world.
See
2003: Major Developments Scheduled for Year. Things to Look Out For and Things to Look Forward To.
